diet.text: Other snakes (including venomous ones), rodents, lizards, eggs

overview.text: The Common or Eastern Kingsnake is a glossy, powerful, non-venomous constrictor of the eastern United States, famous for eating other snakes - including venomous ones such as rattlesnakes, copperheads and cottonmouths, whose venom it appears to resist.

identification.text: Shiny black or dark brown with narrow white or yellow crossbands that split along the sides and link up, giving a chain-like pattern - hence the old name Chain Kingsnake. The amount of pale colour varies from place to place.

size.label: Typical adults
size.text: About 90-122 cm (36-48 in) in total length.

size.label: Largest
size.text: The largest member of its genus, with a maximum recorded total length of 208 cm.

distribution.label: In the narrow sense
distribution.text: As defined by Pyron and Burbrink in 2009, the Eastern Kingsnake ranges from New Jersey south to the Florida Keys and west to the Florida panhandle and south-eastern Alabama.

distribution.label: In the broad sense
distribution.text: Many books and some herpetological societies still use the name *L. getula* for the whole group, which spans much of the United States and northern Mexico. SnakeList's map reflects records under this name.

habitat.text: Uses a wide range of habitats, from pine woods and hardwood forest to the edges of swamps, fields and farmland.

diet.text: A generalist that kills by constriction. Besides snakes, it eats small mammals, birds and their eggs, frogs, lizards, and turtles and their eggs.

taxonomy.text: In 2009 Pyron and Burbrink split the traditional Common Kingsnake into five species: [[lampropeltis-getula|*L. getula*]] (east), [[lampropeltis-nigra|*L. nigra*]] (Mississippi valley), [[lampropeltis-holbrooki|*L. holbrooki*]] (central), *L. splendida* (desert) and [[lampropeltis-californiae|*L. californiae*]] (west). The eastern species includes the former subspecies *getula*, *floridana* and *meansi*.
Not everyone accepts the split: the Southwestern Herpetologists Society, for example, keeps the traditional single species, arguing the split rests mostly on mitochondrial DNA.

similar.text: the Black Kingsnake of the Mississippi valley, mostly black with only faint pale speckling.
the Speckled Kingsnake, which has a pale spot on nearly every scale instead of crossbands.

funfacts.text: The "king" in its name refers to its habit of eating other snakes - even venomous ones, whose venom it appears to shrug off.

zootaxa.title: Systematics of the Common Kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula) and the burden of heritage in taxonomy
